root.note: That Italian casco comes from Spanish casco is well documented. The Spanish word is usually traced to Vulgar Latin quassicare, ‘to break’, but details are debated.

history: Casco, the helmet you must wear on a scooter or at work, is a Spanish loan. Spanish casco first meant a shard of broken pottery and then, by extension, a skull and a helmet, the hard shell around a head. It is usually traced to a Vulgar Latin verb meaning ‘to break’, related to Latin quassare, ‘to shake, to shatter’. Italian borrowed the word in the sixteenth century, at a time when Spanish rulers and soldiers were present in many Italian states. The old Italian word for a helmet, elmo, survives mainly in poetry and history books. Today casco is the general word: casco integrale (full-face), casco da cantiere (hard hat), and caschi blu, the UN peacekeepers.
historyEinfach: Casco means ‘helmet’. Italian took the word from Spanish in the 1500s. In Spanish, casco first meant a broken piece of pottery, then a skull and a helmet. The word probably comes from a Latin verb meaning ‘to break’. You see it in casco integrale and in caschi blu, the ‘blue helmets’ of the UN.

elsewhere.text: French casque, ‘helmet’, also comes from Spanish casco, and English casque (a medieval helmet) comes from French.
